details:
**Hamantaschen**
Triangular filled pastries eaten on Purim. They are said to represent the three-cornered hat of the villain Haman, and are also called "Haman's ears" (oznei Haman) or likened to his pockets.

**Groggers (graggers)**
Noisemakers or rattles that congregants shake, along with shouting and stamping, every time Haman's name is read aloud during the Megillah, symbolically "blotting out" his name.

**Megillah / Book of Esther**
The biblical scroll telling the Purim story, read aloud in synagogue on the holiday. It recounts how Queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai foiled the Persian vizier Haman's plot to massacre the Jews of the Persian Empire.

**Haman**
The wicked chief minister of the Persian king who resented Mordecai's refusal to bow to him and plotted to kill all the Jews. He was ultimately hanged on the very gallows he had built for Mordecai.

**14th of Adar**
The date on which Purim is celebrated in the Hebrew calendar, usually falling in late winter or early spring.

**"Cursed be Haman" and "Blessed be Mordecai"**
The Talmud instructs that on Purim one should drink until one can no longer tell the difference between these two phrases, which is the basis for the holiday's tradition of heavy drinking.

**Mishloach manot (shalach manos)**
Gifts of ready-to-eat food, often baskets including hamantaschen, sent to friends and neighbors on Purim. Giving them is one of the holiday's commandments.

**Shushan Purim**
The version of Purim celebrated a day later, on the 15th of Adar, in cities that were walled in the time of Joshua, such as Jerusalem. It commemorates the Jews of the capital Shushan, who fought their enemies for an extra day.

**Festival of Lots**
The literal meaning of "Purim," from the Hebrew/Akkadian word "pur," meaning lot. It refers to the lots Haman cast to choose the date on which the Jews would be massacred.

**Ten sons of Haman read in one breath**
During the Megillah reading, the reader tries to recite the names of Haman's ten sons in a single breath, symbolizing that they were killed (and hanged) at the same time.

**Mordecai**
Esther's cousin, who raised her as an adopted daughter. He refused to bow to Haman, uncovered a plot against the king, and urged Esther to intercede for her people.

**Vashti**
The first queen of King Ahasuerus. She was banished after refusing his command to appear before his guests at a royal feast, which led to Esther being chosen as the new queen.

**Bigtan and Teresh**
Two royal eunuchs who plotted to assassinate King Ahasuerus. Mordecai overheard and exposed their conspiracy, a deed later recorded in the royal chronicles and rewarded by the king.

**Ahasuerus (Achashverosh)**
The Persian king of the Book of Esther, often identified with Xerxes I. Esther fasted for three days before approaching him unbidden, and then revealed Haman's plot to him.

**Purim Katan and Purim Meshulash**
Special variants of the holiday. Purim Katan ("little Purim") is the 14th of the first Adar in a leap year, when the holiday proper is held in Adar II (seven of every nineteen years); Purim Meshulash ("triple Purim") occurs in Jerusalem when Shushan Purim falls on the Sabbath, spreading observances over three days.
